name: Big Company vs Small Company Engineering
scope: What died with the giants; sign-off culture vs move-fast; semiconductor consolidation from inside

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard in the early 1980s was organised as 82 divisions, each holding a product line and run as a self-contained small company with all the functions of one. Most divisions held 50 to 100 people, the largest, disc memory, about 300, and the structure kept engineering close to its customers even though from executive level the company looked fragmented.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was 82 different divisions and each one had a product and the, and each division was run as a small company
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: The decision to break Hewlett-Packard in two was financial rather than technical: computer businesses commanded higher stock-market multiples than instrument businesses, so separating them was expected to raise the valuation of the computing half.
claims.quote_verbatim: They broke up the company because they, they, they, the, the stock on computers had higher multipliers than the stock on the instruments
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: The Hewlett-Packard split took effect in 1999. The computer and printer business retained the Hewlett-Packard name while the original test-and-measurement business, which the company had been founded on, was renamed Agilent and later Keysight.
claims.quote_verbatim: the world changed in 99 when Hewlett-Packard split up into the computer division
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard started in a Palo Alto garage and its first product, the 200A audio oscillator, was a piece of test equipment; the company is the origin of the garage-startup template later applied across Silicon Valley.
claims.quote_verbatim: their first product, um, 200 day, 200 was a piece of testing equipment
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard gave engineers Friday afternoons for self-directed work decades before Google's 20-percent time made the arrangement famous.
claims.quote_verbatim: They had Friday afternoons to do whatever the hell they wanted to
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Yates - Recondite Radiation Raconteur

claims.claim_text: Bell Labs deliberately mixed electrical and mechanical staff in the same corridors at a time when most companies separated people by discipline, on the reasoning that unplanned conversation across specialties over coffee and lunch produced ideas that neither group would reach alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: Bell Labs intentionally mingled them all together
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Large instrument and research organisations of that era scheduled contact rather than leaving it to chance: a fixed daily 10 a.m. coffee break and a Friday-afternoon beer bust were institutional features of Hewlett-Packard's working culture, in contrast to individually partitioned modern workplaces.
claims.quote_verbatim: the coffee break time, 10 a.m. every day, the bell goes off
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard's product development ran on what was called next-bench syndrome: an engineer built a tool to solve the problem of the engineer at the adjacent bench, giving an immediate local customer whose feedback validated or killed the idea before large sums were committed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd develop a tool that would solve a problem for the guy over on the next bench
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Long-horizon technology work was tolerated inside the large instrument companies to a degree that has no modern equivalent: one Hewlett-Packard technology programme ran sixteen years before appearing in a shipping product, while individual projects could be cancelled abruptly with two years of work behind them.
claims.quote_verbatim: we worked on for 16 years before it actually got into a product
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard's instruments carried bare numeric designations rather than marketed names because the company sold engineer to engineer and did not route product naming through a marketing function.
claims.quote_verbatim: the neat thing about HP is it was selling to other engineers, so we kind of knew our audience
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard ran and published formal research into the optimal legend colours for contrast and fast reading on the front panel of the HP-35 calculator. Later instrument front panels have been coloured on far thinner grounds, including a waveform button made blue because the designers preferred blue.
claims.quote_verbatim: because they famously put a lot of research into what uh text overlay colors would go on the front of the calculator they did a lot of research they did papers on it and everything what is the optimal color for contrast and quick viewing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kismetic Keithley Katowse

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard developed its own standards, architectures and user interfaces, and when IBM's personal computer appeared in 1982 its engineers judged it less capable than machines HP already had and declined to follow. HP only built to the IBM PC specification after that architecture had become dominant, and the course correction took years.
claims.quote_verbatim: when IBM came out with a personal computer in 1982, it really wasn't as powerful as the things that Hewlett-Packard had been developing
claims.speaker: Steve Liebson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Employment contracts at Hewlett-Packard claimed first rights to inventions made by employees. Steve Jobs, working in HP's calculator department on calculator chips, was obliged to offer the Apple I to HP before he could build it himself; HP turned it down.
claims.quote_verbatim: his contract with Hewlett Packard said that every, you know, that he has to give them first rights to ideas that he comes up with
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hipster Fodder

claims.claim_text: Signature analysis was Hewlett-Packard's attempt to systematise digital troubleshooting: known-good behaviour was captured by running dedicated test software on the instrument, and a logic probe at a defined node returned a short four-character signature that the technician compared against the documented value.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would take a note, known good. They had a special device that they would run a special piece of test software and you would hook up a logic probe and it'll give you like a four letter number key
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard test equipment built from roughly the mid-1970s to the mid-1990s carries signature-analysis codes internally, so signature troubleshooting remains available on that whole generation of instruments to anyone who can obtain the data.
claims.quote_verbatim: any, any piece of test equipment from HP from the mid seventies to I'd say the mid nineties has those codes in it
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Signature codes are worthless without the service manual generated against that specific instrument, since the signature is only meaningful compared with the recorded known-good value; losing the documentation strands the diagnostic capability built into the hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't have the manual that's been tested with that specific instrument, then they're just dead weight
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Production testing of analog parameters on analog parts was done with homemade testers rather than universal commercial testers: racks of Hewlett-Packard instruments under GPIB control, assembled and programmed in-house for each part.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had a lot of homemade testers. And some of them were IEEE, rack and stack type things with, you know, a lot of Hewlett Packard equipment
claims.speaker: Art Kay
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Art Kay

claims.claim_text: The HP 8510 was the reference network analyser of its era at roughly a quarter of a million dollars fully loaded, and it was enough of a platform that third parties built and exported add-on boxes for it, including systems for measuring the radar signature of stealth aircraft.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 8510 was the best network analyzer in the world. And, you know, they cost on the order of a quarter million if you buy them fully loaded
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Companies buying in Hewlett-Packard's and IBM's volumes had semiconductor makers silkscreen house part numbers onto otherwise standard parts, so a board can carry a commodity device such as a 74HC00 under an in-house number. This makes repair a matter of identifying the underlying part, and a company running such a scheme for decades can exhaust its own number space.
claims.quote_verbatim: the manufacturer puts the HP part number silkscreen onto the chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: Overhead in a large instrument or medical-device company is easy to underestimate: an internal analysis at one such firm put the fully burdened cost of shipping an empty cardboard box at about three hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: it cost about $300 to ship an empty cardboard box
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: At the largest silicon vendors, design-in attention is reserved for very high-volume customers such as Dell and Hewlett-Packard or the contract manufacturers building for them; smaller designers interact with the catalogue rather than with the vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: to get their attention, you need to be a, you know, a super high-volume manufacturer. A Dell or a HP
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: Above roughly fifty thousand machines, buyers stop purchasing conventional 19-inch enterprise servers from Hewlett-Packard or Dell because the price carries plastics, front panels and per-machine status displays that serve no purpose in a room nobody visits; at that scale the specification is rewritten around what the operator actually observes.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start to realize that you're paying for a lot, especially things like plastics and front panels
claims.speaker: Rick Altherr
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Rick Altherr

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard engineered its calculators to be correct in the final displayed digit, while Sinclair deliberately accepted results that were only approximately right in order to reach a low price point. The same accuracy-versus-cost split separates instrument grades generally.
claims.quote_verbatim: Hewlett Packard went to all this work to make their calculators, like, you know, accurate to the last digit
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: The HP-15C of the Voyager landscape-format calculator series shipped from about 1982 until the end of the decade and was later reissued after a sustained campaign by users, showing that a discontinued design can be brought back when its user base is organised enough to make the demand visible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it came out in about 82 or something and it finished and they actually produced it up until the end of the 80s
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard released one of its older calculator designs as open source, publishing schematics and supporting design material.
claims.quote_verbatim: Basically they open source. One of their older designs. With schematics and everything else
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Big Business Buffoonery

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard developed the memristor and pursued commercialisation with a Korean memory manufacturer, but a corporate research announcement should be treated as a product only once the part can be ordered from a distributor.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll believe it when I can buy a chip from DigiKey
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Love Robots and Pantyhose Screens

claims.claim_text: Hewlett-Packard announced it would divest its personal-computer business and step back from consumer products, the reasoning being that consumer-level margins were not worth competing for.
claims.quote_verbatim: They don't want to play with consumer margins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Yates - Recondite Radiation Raconteur

claims.claim_text: Printer makers authenticate consumables with a chip in the cartridge. Third-party cartridges sold as chipped are still detected as non-genuine and produce a warranty warning, though they continue to function.
claims.quote_verbatim: the printer's able to detect it and says this is not a genuine cartridge
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Tektronix was vertically integrated to the point of manufacturing its own cathode ray tubes, and supplied instruments with ceramic terminal strips and matching silver solder in the box, so a period Tektronix instrument exposes the entire manufacturing stack of the company that built it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they built CRTs in-house
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: Tektronix's late-1970s one-gigahertz purely analog oscilloscope originated as a request from the United States Atomic Energy Commission for nuclear weapons testing. Tektronix agreed on terms of thirty thousand dollars per unit, then the price of a house, a thousand-unit commitment from the customer, and the right to sell the resulting instrument on the open market afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're going to cost $30,000. You're going to, you're going to have to buy a thousand of them
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: The earliest Tektronix instruments, the 511 through 514, were grey; the blue that became the company's signature arrived with the 535 series. Touch-up spray paint in that specific Tektronix blue is still sold for restoration work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 535 series ended up being, ended up being that blue
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: The performance gap between the incumbent oscilloscope makers and low-cost entrants rests on silicon: Tektronix and Agilent develop custom acquisition ASICs, while low-cost USB instruments are assembled from commodity parts and therefore advance only as fast as commodity silicon does.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're not making custom silicon like a tech or an agilent does
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: Those in-house instrument ASICs stay in service for decades. Tektronix has been reported to still use an ASIC designed thirty years earlier, and scope designers deliberately keep older silicon on mature processes rather than requalify a signal path.
claims.quote_verbatim: tech are famously still using the ASIC from 30 years ago
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fan Fanboys

claims.claim_text: Spectrum functions grafted onto an oscilloscope architecture inherit its sweep behaviour: on a Tektronix MDO3000 in RF mode, narrowing the resolution bandwidth to 300 Hz or below over a low-megahertz span stretches a single update out to tens of minutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: set the uh resolution bandwidth filter to 300 hertz or below
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: Entry-level oscilloscope pricing held around seven to eight hundred dollars across thirty years of magazine advertising. The floor is held deliberately, since a vendor dropping below it undercuts the rest of its own range.
claims.quote_verbatim: even over 30 years, the entry level price was, you know, around that seven, $800 figure
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: The incumbent instrument makers effectively withdrew from the low-end oscilloscope market once cheap capable instruments became widely available; Tektronix had previously served that segment with rebadged product such as the TDS-220 rather than its own design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Tech have given up on low-end scopes, I think, basically
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: The secondhand market for current-model instruments is thin and badly priced: a 300 MHz four-channel Tektronix DPO4034 with probes plus a Fluke 87, a package listing near ten thousand dollars new, changed hands privately for five hundred dollars while its resale value was six to seven thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: He scored a 300 megahertz Tektronix DPO 4034 four-channel scope with probes and a Fluke 87 for 500 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: Fluke enforces trade dress on the yellow multimeter holster. Threatened by Fluke's lawyers, Tektronix changed a meter's holster from yellow to blue rather than test the claim in court, leaving two otherwise identical Tektronix meters distinguished only by holster colour. The trade-dress claim itself has never been adjudicated.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I've got two identical Tektronix multimeters here. One's got a yellow holster. One's got a blue holster
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: Tektronix, Keithley and Fluke came under common ownership by Danaher, placing much of the mid-range test and measurement market inside a single holding structure.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're all under the same group. They're all owned by the E. Will Danaher Group
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: Assurances that an acquired instrument company will keep its own culture are testable against what happens to its site and brand: the Keithley facility was rebranded Tektronix after the acquisition.
claims.quote_verbatim: I still drive by the Keithley facility, which now happens to be branded techtronics
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: Tektronix's Beaverton campus was progressively sold off as the company contracted; Xerox bought the printer operation and moved onto the same campus, and Nike occupies other former Tektronix buildings, which are still referred to by their Tektronix building numbers.
claims.quote_verbatim: They just bought that part of Tektronix and moved in
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Factory parts support for TM500-era Tektronix equipment has ended, so keeping that surviving instrument base alive now depends on scavenging or fabricating parts. This is a direct present-day cost to users of the vendor consolidation that removed the original service organisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't call up tektronics and get parts for it anymore
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Twelfth Day of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: Instrument makers specified semi-custom silicon under house part numbers, as in the Tektronix TDS220 whose custom part was manufactured by National Semiconductor. No public data exists for such devices, and the best a repairer can do is identify the standard part the design derives from and work from that.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got some custom part number. It's manufactured by National Semiconductor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Even the dominant oscilloscope manufacturer distributed other companies' instruments through its national subsidiaries where its own range did not cover a market segment; Tektronix Australia sold a competitor's scope alongside its own.
claims.quote_verbatim: Tektronix Australia were actually selling some other brands, company, oscilloscope
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Boeing, PCBs & Startups - Awful Airplane Aeration

claims.claim_text: The American semiconductor industry descends from Shockley through Fairchild: Noyce and Moore left Fairchild to found Intel, National Semiconductor came from the same lineage, and Linear Technology in turn spun out of National.
claims.quote_verbatim: And that was Noyce and more. And they split out to do Intel. And then also National Semiconductor came out of there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: My Kind of Town

claims.claim_text: Analog semiconductor firms were funded and governed by a small overlapping group: one co-founder of National Semiconductor was also involved in funding Linear Technology and chaired the boards of Cypress, Microchip and Vitesse.
claims.quote_verbatim: Pierre was a co-founder of National Semiconductor, was involved in the funding of linear technology, was chairman of the board of Cypress, Microchip, Vitesse
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor manufacturing in Silicon Valley left physical liabilities behind: the former National Semiconductor site is now a contaminated brownfield rather than an operating plant.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's where National Semiconductor used to be. And now it's a brown site
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: After Texas Instruments absorbed National Semiconductor the National data sheets were reissued under TI branding, typically by scripting a TI cover page onto the original document. Documents therefore circulate in hybrid form, with National URLs at the foot of pages carrying TI logos at the top.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've rebranded everything. And their data sheets are weird now
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: Post-merger layoffs at Texas Instruments followed from portfolio overlap with National Semiconductor rather than from financial distress; consolidation eliminates duplicated roles across two catalogues that address the same markets.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're just consolidating because there was huge overlap there with National
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Chip design headcount is the last thing cut in a semiconductor consolidation, because analog and silicon design skill disperses irreversibly once released and cannot be rebuilt on demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're probably not letting go many of the chip designers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments issued last-time-buy notices covering roughly a hundred parts tied to one old National Semiconductor plant, including long-lived audio devices such as the LM386. Parts of that age end not because demand disappears but because the specific fab that makes them closes.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have, you know, probably 100 chips or so that are manufactured in some specific old national semiconductor plant somewhere
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Consolidation in analog silicon has left effectively two large independent vendors; Linear Technology was absorbed by Analog Devices, so a jelly-bean function such as a charge-pump inverter that once had many independent second sources now has variants under only a couple of corporate roofs.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's chip company one and chip company two and sadly there's only two left
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Proof Of Blink

claims.claim_text: Before microprocessors were available, a small company could commission a full-custom integrated circuit from National Semiconductor for about one hundred thousand dollars, in this case a 200-gate-equivalent part. The programme was delivered a year late, which for a small company was fatal to the product it was intended for.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were going to make for us a full custom silicon part. And I think it was $100,000
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: Hiring at the large semiconductor firms tracked business cycles rather than individual need: a 1974 graduate recruited by National Semiconductor was laid off after about two months, the company having spent more relocating him to California than it paid him in wages.
claims.quote_verbatim: They worked me for about two months, and then I got laid off
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments still runs its own fabs. A vertically integrated vendor aggregates its own product lines into internal scale at the wafer level, so any one order is a slice of a much larger run, which a fabless competitor bidding for foundry capacity cannot reproduce.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI has their own fab. But if they're all, if they're all fabless, then it's, there's no scale there
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Fab ownership shows up in allocation. In the 2008 shortage Linear Technology, which ran its own fabs, quoted lead times around 30 weeks on parts for which Texas Instruments was quoting 99.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI was talking 99 weeks, and linear's talking 30
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Merging two semiconductor vendors correlates supply risk that used to be independent: when the surviving catalogue runs through common processes and fabs, a single problem propagates across every product line at once, whereas separate companies with different processes failed at different times.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the product lines of these two companies look the same
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: New fab investment is aimed at leading-edge nodes, while the parts that went unobtainable in the shortage were made on mature processes and older wafer sizes whose domestic capacity had been moved offshore once it stopped paying for itself. Rebuilding leading-edge capacity does not restore availability of those parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want TI to reopen their, their Richardson plant to full capacity
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments financed its fab expansion with borrowed money against an expectation of five to six billion dollars in annual revenue once the capacity is fully operational, a payback horizon measured in years rather than product cycles.
claims.quote_verbatim: expected to generate five to six billion in revenue annually for the company once it's fully operational
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Histogrammic or Histomagraphical

claims.claim_text: A wafer-size transition does not lower part prices for the buyer, because the capital cost of the new fab, on the order of seven billion dollars for the 450 mm generation, is recovered through the parts it produces.
claims.quote_verbatim: the price of chips isn't gonna drop, because somebody's gotta pay for that $7 billion capital investment
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: Before the internet the vendor data book was the only design information available, so the vendors that handed data books out freely or sold them through local shops were designed into products, while those that restricted them lost sockets. This is the mechanism behind the long-lived preference for National and TI parts among engineers of that generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got, you know, national data books on your bookshelf, well, you're going to be using their parts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Access to information from the large semiconductor companies was mediated by field sales representatives, so obtaining a data sheet or a sample could require negotiating with an intermediary and was gated on projected volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: the in-between sales reps between these companies that you have to interface with all the time to get a data sheet sometimes or get a sample part
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments once ran a single large technical conference that functioned as a week of concentrated electronics education framed as a sales event, and it determined the part choices of attendees for more than a decade afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: you folks used to have the very best electronics education conference in the world disguised as a sales pitch
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: The format that made that conference effective was one engineer per part who had actually designed a product with it, present to answer questions and issue development kits. Splitting or dropping such an event removes the principal route to introductions and documentation for parts that are otherwise hard to learn.
claims.quote_verbatim: every part for sale had an expert who had designed a product with that part on hand for you to ask questions, to give you free development kits
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments staffs its public E2E forums with the applications engineers who design and work with the products, some spending ten to twenty hours a week answering there, which makes the forum rather than the sales channel the practical support route for a small customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: I spend like 10 to 20 hours a week on the forums
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors differ structurally in whom they can serve. Some deliberately build only for tier-one accounts, and Texas Instruments built application and sales structures to support customers of any size. The problem case is a vendor that keeps its tier-one focus but sells to smaller customers anyway without the structure to support them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get other guys like TI who support everybody, and they've got their application structure and their sales structure and everything set up to do that
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Service from a large vendor scales with what the customer can spend, but a startup can still obtain samples and field-engineering attention by making its product into a story the vendor's own marketing can retell later.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can convince them that your product is really great. I mean, they're going to go to bat for you and get you samples
claims.speaker: John Davis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Davis

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments is organised into strongly separated vertical business units, with sensor teams and processor teams working independently. A consequence for the customer is that every chip carries its own reference design and the board designer becomes the integrator of the surrounding catalogue parts himself.
claims.quote_verbatim: the guys that work on sensors don't talk to anybody else in the company
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_03
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Documentation released by a large semiconductor vendor is filtered on projected support cost: a chapter covering the programmable real-time units was removed from a Texas Instruments technical reference manual on management review as likely to generate too much technical support, then republished separately through BeagleBoard with the explicit caveat that TI would not answer questions on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the chapter that was originally written for the technical reference manual that had been removed after being kind of reviewed by managers
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner And Robert
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: A silicon vendor can withdraw software support while the part remains in production, forcing designs already committed to the processor off the vendor SDK and onto a third-party board support package.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because of some limitations in TI's, almost complete dropping of software support for their chips, I have to switch from the TI SDK to this Ridge Run one
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Third-party board-support vendors fill the gap left when a silicon vendor drops software support, covering most of a processor catalogue with better documentation and paid support at roughly five thousand dollars a licence, which for a small team amounts to buying an employee.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's like five grand for the license
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Capital expenditure thresholds inside large companies require sign-off above a fixed amount, so a buyer will take the cheapest instrument that clears the limit and add bandwidth or features later as separate smaller purchases. This procurement structure is why instrument vendors sell software-unlockable upgrades.
claims.quote_verbatim: most big companies will have... If it's over that limit, then it has to go get approved by
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Negotiated part pricing still applies at hundred-thousand-piece volumes and is unavailable below that, and customers who must buy a full reel to obtain it commonly push the unused inventory onto their assembler to hold.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need a discount on, you know, this TI part because I'm buying a hundred thousand of them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors will trade discounts on the order of fifteen to twenty percent for cash paid up front, since a supplier will always take cash today over cash later. A cash-rich customer therefore uses prepayment as an investment vehicle as much as a purchasing arrangement.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're getting like a 15, 20% discount or whatever
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Compare and Contrast Tech Entitlement - Worldly Working Wonks

claims.claim_text: During allocation, offering higher volume does not move a small customer up a semiconductor vendor's priority list. Lead times are quoted flat, in this case two months, with the instruction to plan further ahead, because the vendor is scheduling wafer starts rather than shipping from distributor stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: look, is there any volume that I can give you that will bump me up the priority list
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Sipping Coulombs

claims.claim_text: When integrated parts from a major vendor become unobtainable and automotive-qualified stock disappears first, one response for a design that is not space constrained is to trade board area back for availability, rebuilding a function such as a switching converter from a small microcontroller, an op-amp and a pass transistor that can still be sourced.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI parts are very hard for me to find right now. Anything automotive obviously is out the window
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Toasted Marshmallow Connectors

claims.claim_text: Counterfeit parts are silkscreened with genuine vendor branding, since the marking cost is negligible against the price of the part being imitated, so package markings are not evidence of provenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: Not only are they fake, but they, they, they actually brand them as TI
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Recent integrated parts arrive in vendor-proprietary packages that competitors are not permitted to copy, so there is no drop-in second source. A single part choice therefore carries far more schedule and supply risk than an equivalent decision in the era of standard packages.
claims.quote_verbatim: TI owns that footprint or microchip owns that footprint
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: Exclusivity contracts that bar a semiconductor vendor from selling a given part to anyone but one customer are a deeper obstacle to independent repair than withheld schematics or service tools, because no amount of documentation makes an unpurchasable part replaceable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't buy that part Even though it's a TI part Or something TI can only sell that To Apple
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: AI aren't sentient yet...right?

claims.claim_text: Expired patents on the 8051 architecture allow any vendor to embed the core without a licence fee, which is why it persists inside modern radio system-on-chips such as the Texas Instruments CC2540 long after it stopped being competitive on its merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's because the patents have expired. You don't have to pay a license fee to anyone
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Magical Fire Bags

claims.claim_text: Two opposing positions coexist inside large semiconductor firms: patenting publishes the method and lets competitors design around it, so a technique may be better hidden in the silicon, while top-down pressure to generate patentable work persists because patent counts are presented to shareholders.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you patent something, it becomes public and people can see how you did it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Industry standards bodies are contested by semiconductor vendors trying to get proprietary features written into the specification so that their silicon becomes the compliant choice, with tactics extending to bringing extra members to voting sessions and holding pre-meetings to set strategy.
claims.quote_verbatim: some companies, like TI or, you know, whoever, would do things like stacking the committee votes
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Major semiconductor manufacturers report digital power control, and often motor control with it, as a distinct revenue segment, which is a direct signal of how large those markets have become relative to the general catalogue.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually report that as a separate market because it's a huge market
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: From Boston In Boxers?

claims.claim_text: The Texas Instruments calculator division sustained margins far above the rest of the company, selling for around one hundred and fifty dollars a product costing roughly five to build, which left it with discretionary money that other divisions did not have.
claims.quote_verbatim: make a $5 calculator and charge $154
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: Vendor design tools are pitched at one audience and cannot satisfy both: the simplified WebBench power-supply flow gave newcomers an answer in minutes while frustrating experienced designers who wanted inductor data, topology comparison and waveforms of the kind SPICE provides.
claims.quote_verbatim: I remember it was super, super, super simple. And I used to hate it because it was just like, it felt very kid-like
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Duff

claims.claim_text: Training material written for internal use at Texas Instruments, such as a four-part course on op-amp stability, circulates publicly and is substantive design instruction rather than promotional material.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a course that's given internally at TI
claims.episode_title: All the way with DLJ

claims.claim_text: Where a part implements a published standard such as USB Power Delivery, development information issued by one vendor can be applied directly to a competitor's controller. Code written against the standard rather than the vendor library also survives an end-of-life part swap.
claims.quote_verbatim: he went to a Texas instruments part, which was another type of type C, you know, a competing device. And he used their development information
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: Vendor-sponsored reference stacks accelerate a proof of concept only while the design stays on the exact listed module and processor. Substituting a neighbouring part number or adding one unsupported requirement puts the team back into greenfield integration, often after the schedule has already been committed on the strength of the demonstration.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to, you know, integrate your one special thing or use that really unique processor, well, good luck
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Alternate Info Sources

claims.claim_text: Large chip companies design on the commercial EDA tools, principally Cadence and Mentor, so experience with open-source ASIC design software counts as familiarity with the flow rather than as a matching skill when applying.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you try to go to TI and be like, well, I learned on electric, right? This open source chip design program. They're like, well, we use Cadence
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Above a certain size a company builds its own component libraries and footprint data internally rather than buying it, which caps the addressable market for selling such data to precisely the customers least able to pay.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they're sufficiently large enough, they'll just develop an in-house and just do it themselves
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: Large electronics companies increasingly spin and hand-build prototype boards internally rather than through a contract line, and the parts involved push stencil requirements toward cut features in the tens of microns.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've seen a huge jump in clientele from large electronics companies, big name companies that are prototyping and, you know, spinning multiple boards in house that they're hand building
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: An engineer trained through Hewlett-Packard and then FAA- and FDA-certified products treats prototype work assembled from modules as categorically different from production work, and states explicitly that a qualified electrical engineer must vet the system before volume, rather than letting a working prototype pass as a design.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to go to production with this, I want you to find a nice double E who can vet this system
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Crossovers and Call-ins

claims.claim_text: Informal environments substitute drive-by opinion for structured design review. A passer-by proposing a different switching regulator weeks before an engineering-validation build carries none of the schedule risk of the change, which is the specific defect that a formal review with named owners removes.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone from the incubator walked through. And they looked down. They're like, oh, you're using a Texas Instruments switching regulator
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: A growing hardware company faces an explicit choice between adding business units and keeping the working conditions that produced its output. SparkFun addressed the question deliberately as a company, with Hewlett-Packard's trajectory as the reference case, and chose to cap growth rather than lose the environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: at some point Hewlett Packard made the decision to just keep adding business units
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: After Texas Instruments acquired ChipCon for a couple of hundred million dollars, the founder ran the resulting TI division for about a year before leaving, a common pattern where the person suited to building a small company is not suited to operating a division of a large one.
claims.quote_verbatim: he continued for another year leading that, basically leading a division of Texas Instruments
claims.speaker: Oyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Regional engineering clusters persist through the mechanism of employees leaving a large anchor employer, taking the proceeds, and starting a firm nearby because they already live there. Aerospace and instrument anchors around Everett and Beaverton seeded exactly that pattern.
claims.quote_verbatim: works at a big technology place, then they make some money and they decide to do their own thing
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: Instrument makers recruited directly in one another's towns, Fluke advertising for engineers in the Denver and Boulder area near Hewlett-Packard's Loveland division and hiring on the spot, since the specialised talent pool was already concentrated there.
claims.quote_verbatim: I saw an ad for Fluke advertising for engineers. And so I went to an interview in downtown Denver, and they hired me on the spot
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Taylor - Multi-talented Meter Maker

claims.claim_text: Motorola priced the 6800 microprocessor at about two hundred and fifty dollars with its peripheral interface adapter at about five. Engineers at the companies visited wanted the technology, but at that processor price their employers concluded they could not build a product around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the PIA were selling for $5 or something, right? They were selling the 6800 for $250
claims.speaker: Chuck Peddle
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Chuck Peddle - Charismatic Chipmaking Coryphaeus

claims.claim_text: New silicon was introduced to the large companies by sending factory staff to run classes for their assembled engineering teams; Hewlett-Packard, Tektronix, NCR and Ford were taught what a microprocessor was and how to wire one up in exactly that format.
claims.quote_verbatim: bring somebody in from the factory, and they'll bring all their engineers together, and you sit down and explain to them what a microprocessor is and how to use it
claims.speaker: Chuck Peddle
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Chuck Peddle - Charismatic Chipmaking Coryphaeus

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments released the 5400 logic family in 1964 for military use; the commercial 7400 equivalent followed about two years later, and integrated circuits do not appear in hobby and commercial magazine projects until 1967.
claims.quote_verbatim: I started with 1964, okay, because that's when the 5400 series was released
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: B Plus Boards and D Minus Cities - Uneath Urban Ubication

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments made high-power 900-nanometre gallium arsenide infrared LEDs at Richardson, north of Dallas, in the era when they were new, and an interested outsider could reach the responsible research scientist directly by writing to the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: Texas Instruments was just north of Dallas, Richardson, Texas. They were making these high-power infrared LEDs, 900-nanometer LEDs out of gallium arsenide
claims.speaker: Forrest Mims
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Forrest Mims - Snell Solisequious Scientist

claims.claim_text: Texas Instruments held the trademark on the term sprite, so Commodore's engineers were required to call the same graphics feature a movable object block.
claims.quote_verbatim: We weren't supposed to say sprite. We were supposed to say movable object block
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: An early-1980s PCB CAD company such as Cadnetics had to design its own workstation hardware as well as write the software, because no standard machine could run that class of code. The window in which vertical integration of this kind was necessary was short, and firms that committed to it were stranded when standard machines arrived.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the day when you had to actually design your own workstation in addition to writing the code
claims.speaker: Steve Liebson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Moving from the bit-slice 2900 family to the single-chip CMOS 29000 replaced a per-design instruction set with a fixed one, which is what allowed standard compilers, in-circuit emulators and a supporting tool ecosystem to exist at all; the CMOS process also ran far cooler than the bipolar parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was a fixed instruction set as opposed to every 2900 design was a different instruction set. So you could have standard compilers and in-circuit emulators and a development ecosystem could grow up around it
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Laser printers from Hewlett-Packard and Apple were the volume applications that briefly made the AMD 29000 one of the highest-shipping CPUs, an illustration that processor volume of that era came from office peripherals rather than computers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the biggest wins for 29000 were HP and Apple who used it in their laser printers
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Military and long-life industrial programmes require written commitments from semiconductor suppliers that a part will still be supported in ten to fifteen years, and extracting those statements from a vendor is slow and difficult even when it is ultimately possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to guarantee 10, 15-year lifespans on actually supporting these products
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: Long-term parameter drift is specified only on selected premium products; an ordinary op-amp carries no long-term stability specification at all, which matters when the equipment it sits in is expected to hold calibration for a decade in an industrial installation.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really on the big products that they spec it out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: Substituting a different manufacturer for an electrically identical part must still be recorded against the build, because lot-level differences between manufacturers only become visible as field failures and are untraceable without that record. High-end CAD tools support approved alternates so purchasing can choose freely within a vetted set.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're going to swap in a different vendor, a different manufacturing part number, even if it's the same electrically similar part, you should notate that in some way
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

attribution_notes: This bundle is depth-relaxed: 226 of 300 passages are graded 'mention', and most of the historical material about HP, Tektronix, National Semiconductor and TI sits in those passages rather than in the graded 'explains' set.
Speaker attribution follows speaker_repaired and is set to null wherever the passage carries FUSED or UNRELIABLE-ATTR, including the TI conference passages from ep442 and the ep369 HP garage passage.

ep273 and ep310 passages asserting that Texas Instruments bought Maxim and Linear Technology were not used; ep404 in the same bundle corrects the acquirer of Linear Technology to Analog Devices, and that passage was used instead.
ep215 passage attributing Infineon to a Hewlett-Packard spinoff was not used; the speaker retracts the claim within the same passage.
